targets.syllabus: Part 1: Course Information Course: ISE 331: Computer Security Fundamentals Semester: Spring 2026 Main Instructor name: Amir Rahmati Co-Instructor name: Xinrui Yu Course hours: Class 01: Tuesday 2:00 PM - 3:35 PM, Thursday 8:00 AM - 9:35 AM, Week 1-14 Class 02: Tuesday 3:50 PM - 5:25 PM, Thursday 9:50 AM - 11:25 AM, Week 1-14 Office hours: Lixi Building 201-4 Mon 09:30 – 11:00, 11:30 – 12:30 Tue 11:30 – 12:30 Thu 11:30 – 12:30 Fri 09:30 – 11:00 Prerequisites: Basic understanding of Computer Architecture, Networks, and OS Course Description: Introduces the basic concepts and terminology of computer security. Covers basic security topics such as cryptography, operating systems security, network security, and language- based security. Major Topics Covered: • Basic Crypto • System Security • Network Security • Web Security • OS Security • Mobile Security • Forensics • Human Factors • Emerging Threats • Authentication • Access Control • Privacy • Cloud Security Required Course Textbook and Materials: Principles of Computer Security: CompTIA Security + and Beyond (5e, William Arthur Conklin, Greg White, Chuck Cothren, Roger Davis, Dwayne Williams, McGraw-Hill, 2018. ISBN: 978-1260026016) Course Delivery: Lixi Building 403 How We Will Communicate: Email: amir.rahmati@stonybrook.edu, xryu47@gmail.com Part 2: Course Learning Objectives Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: 1) Conversant with the basic terminology and concepts of computer security. 2) Understand basic security threats to systems and networks. 3) Be familiar with basic strategies used to protect systems and networks. 4) Be able to analyze, design, and build secure systems of basic complexity. targets.midterm_guide: -Midterm Exam Preparation Guide Syllabus: The midterm exam will be based on Weeks 1 to 5. Weeks 6 and 7 are not included. Exam Structure: Section I: 6 Fill-in-the-blank Questions (2 points each) Section 2: 10 MCQs (2 points each) Section 3: 3 Analysis Problems (10 points each) Section 4: 1 Modeling question (12 points) Section 5: 3 Analysis Questions (26 points total) Tips: All fill in the blank questions are based glossary of the key terms from week 1. All MCQs are from week 2. Section 3: One question about usability. 👉 Review usability concepts from week 1. One question about designing for usability. 👉 Review the section “Focus on the human” from week 2 One question about cognitive processes. 👉 Focus on conceptual understanding of various cognitive processes covered in week 5. Section 4: One modeling question based on Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) and Task Frequency Analysis. 👉 Focus on the section “Know the Users and Tasks”. Section 5: One question is about Task-Artifact Cycle. 👉 Review the section “User Needs” from week 1. One question is based on section 1.9.3 - Design Principles ( chapter 1 - What’s Interaction Design?) One question about analyzing and selecting interaction types for a given system. (chapter 03 – conceptualizing interaction) Sample Questions: 1. Explain how users acquire mental models through: Interaction Explanation 2. Modeling Question: Scenario: A local grocery store wants to create a new app. Customers currently struggle to buy groceries online because the search is slow, the checkout is confusing, and they often forget items. The store wants to understand exactly how a customer shops before they build the app. Using Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) and Task Frequency Analysis, analyze the task of Order groceries online. a) Main Goal Write the main goal of the user. Example: Buy groceries using the mobile app. b) Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) Break the main goal into five subtasks in the correct order. Open the grocery app. Search for specific food items. ... ... ... c) Simple HTA Structure Draw a simple chart showing: The Main Goal at the very top. The Subtasks connected underneath it in order. d) Task Frequency Analysis For each subtask you listed in part (b), assign a frequency label: Very Often, Often, Sometimes, or Rarely. 3. The task-artifact cycle explains how technology is designed, used, and improved over time based on people’s needs. Draw a simple diagram to show how the task-artifact cycle works. Label the main parts clearly (people’s needs, technology design, use, and improvement). Explain the task-artifact cycle using a food delivery app as an example. (Write 2–3 simple sentences. Think about how user needs lead to new features and how the app improves over time.) Tip: Think about how food delivery apps started with basic ordering and later added features like live tracking, ratings, and multiple payment options. 4. A student is using a new mobile app for the first time. Read the situations below and answer the questions that follow. Situations: The student focuses only on the “Sign Up” button and ignores other information on the screen. The student remembers their password from the last time they used a similar app. The student understands that a magnifying glass icon means “search.” The student chooses between “Sign Up” and “Log In.” After using the app a few times, the student becomes faster at completing tasks. For each situation, identify the cognitive process being used (Attention, Memory, Perception, Decision-making, Learning) and briefly explain your answer in one sentence. 5. You are designing an information booth in a university library. Students can use it to find available books, reserve study rooms, and ask for library help. Based on the interaction types (instructing, conversing, manipulating, exploring, responding): (a) Which interaction type would you choose for the information booth? (b) Give one reason why your choice would make it easier for students to use the booth. 6. Pick an everyday app or website you use often (such as a shopping app, music app, or banking app). Evaluate its design using the principles below: Feedback: The system gives a clear response after a user action (e.g., a message or animation after clicking a button) Visibility: Important options and information are easy to see and find. Match each situation in Column A with the correct design principle in Column B. Write the correct letter (A–D) next to each number.

practice.01_Crypto_Practice_Questions_Solutions.p: ISE 331: Fundamentals of Computer Security Practice Problems for Cryptography: Lecture 03 to Lecture 08 Directions: Below is a set of exercises and problems you should do for practice. Answering this set of questions should be just one part of your preparation for quizzes and exams. In addition to solving these problems you should: • Review the lecture notes. • Review your homework assignments. • Form a study group and test each other on the material. Note: The solution is provided on the last page. It is strongly recommended that you work on the questions first before going to the solution. Part I. Multiple Choice 1. Which of the following is necessary for the One-Time Pad to achieve perfect confidentiality? A. Every possible key must be equally likely. B. The key must be reused for multiple messages. C. The cipher must operate on fixed-size blocks of data. D. The key must be generated by a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). 2. Which is NOT a property of modern symmetric encryption using block cipher? A. Sender and receiver share the same key B. Can not be brute forced C. Ciphertext does not reveal plaintext D. Reversible with the correct key 3. Alice writes down the hash values of all her important documents. Assume that she is using a secure hash function. Which of the following is probably true? A. If her documents are deleted, she can recover her documents from the hash values. B. If she has a few hundred documents, she has a high chance of discovering two hash values being the same. C. If her documents are modified, she can notice by checking the new hash values against the old ones. D. If two of her documents are similar, their hash values will also be similar. 4. A developer is designing a system to store user passwords on a server. They recall that both encryption and hashing can be used to store the passwords. Which of the following statements best explains why hashing is preferred over encryption? A. Hashing generates fixed length data, but the ciphertext can have different lengths. B. Encrypted password can be recovered with a key, but hashed password cannot be recovered. C. Ciphertexts for the same password can be different, but hashing the same password always gives the same result. D. Encryption of passwords may be slow for a secure encryption algorithm, but hashing of passwords is always fast. 5. Bob is trying to send a 10GB file to Alice efficiently, and he wants the file to remain confidential. Which is the best option? A. Send a key to Alice, use symmetric encryption to encrypt the file, and send the ciphertext B. Exchange a key with Alice with key exchange protocol, then use symmetric encryption to encrypt the file, send ciphertext C. Sign the file with Digital Signature Algorithm, and send the file in plaintext D. Send the file with asymmetric encryption 6. Alice and Bob want to send messages to each other with asymmetric encryption. Which statement below is correct? A. Alice needs to use her secret key to encrypt her message to Bob. B. Bob needs to use his secret key to verify Alice’s public key. C. Alice needs to use both public keys to send and receive messages. D. Bob needs to use his secret key to decrypt Alice’s message. 7. The Diffie-Hellman protocol is primarily used to: A. Create a shared secret over insecure channel. B. Generate a random number for symmetric encryption. C. Sign a message to prove its origin. D. Encrypt long messages in blocks. 8. A malicious attacker obtained a root Certificate Authority’s private key. Which of the following is correct? A. The attacker can revoke all certificates issued by the root CA. B. The attacker can sign certificates for his own websites as the root CA. C. The attacker can decrypt all messages using a certificate from the root CA. D. The attacker can modify the public keys of the root CA. 9. Which prevents Man-in-the-Middle attack in asymmetric encryption? A. The attacker cannot use the public keys of the CAs. B. The CAs will not sign the attacker’s public key. C. The clients will only use the CA’s public key. D. The attacker cannot obtain the CA’s private key. 10. TLS is not used for: A. Determine key exchange algorithm B. Send certificates signed by CAs C. Establish symmetric encryption communication D. Sending account ID and password for login Part II. True or False 1. The security of the One-Time Pad is based on the assumption that no efficient algorithm exists to break it within reasonable time. 2. For modern block ciphers, a change of one bit in the plaintext will result in the change of one random bit in the ciphertext. 3. Unlike symmetric encryption, hash functions do not require a secret key to compute the result. 4. Using Encrypt-and-MAC (sending both the ciphertext and a MAC of the plaintext) guarantees both confidentiality and integrity of the message. 5. A cryptographic hash function that provides 256 bits of output, like SHA-256, offers 256 bits of security against collision attacks. This means an attacker would need to perform approximately 2256 operations to find a collision. 6. In asymmetric encryption, if an attacker obtained Alice’s secret key, the attacker can sign a message as if it is sent by Alice. 7. The root Certificate Authorities (root CAs) are responsible for signing all website certificates. 8. Websites like Baidu and Taobao will not send you messages unless you send them valid certificates first. 9. TLS is responsible for protecting both the confidentiality and integrity of the messages. 10. Current TLS supports multiple symmetric encryption and message authentication algorithms. Part III. Short Answer 1. For a block cipher, the Electronic Code Book (ECB) mode just separate the plaintext into equal-sized blocks, encrypt them with the same key, and concatenate the ciphertext blocks. This operation mode has a security weakness. Explain the cause and danger of this weakness. 2. Alice sends a plaintext p and its hash value h (h = h(p)) to Bob on the channel. The hash function is a secure hash function, like SHA- 256. Bob receives p and h, he calculates h’ = h(p) himself. Seeing that h’ = h, he thinks that p is not modified in transit. Can this method be used to protect the integrity of p against an attacker that can modify what’s on the channel? Explain. 3. Asymmetric encryption is known to need much longer keys to reach the same level of security compared to symm etric encryption. Explain why we still use asymmetric encryption. 4. A server uses salt for password storage. The salt 𝑠 is a random bit sequence. ℎ is a secure hash function. The server performs calculation: 𝑟 = 𝑠 𝐗𝐎𝐑 ℎ(𝑝𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑑), and store 𝑟 with 𝑠 in their database. Does this prevent an offline attacker from performing a dictionary attack? 5. What is a "Trapdoor One-Way Function," and how does it relate to asymmetric encryption? Part IV. Calculation 1. The standard Data Encryption Standard (DES) uses a 56-bit key. A hacker can brute-force all possible keys in 1 day. Assume all conditions remain the same, how long can this hacker brute-force all possible keys if the algorithm uses 112-bit keys instead? Use the approximation 210 ≈ 103. Part I Solution: 1-5 ABCBB 6-10 DABDD Part II Solution: 1-5 FFTFF 6-10 TFFTT Part III Solution: 1. The main weakness in the ECB mode is that identical plaintext blocks will encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks, revealing statistical information of the plaintext. 2. No, following Kerckhoff’s principle, the attacker also knows the hash function. He can just modify p to his own p”, and modify h to his own h”, h” = h(p”). Bob will not notice anything wrong upon receiving p” and h”, since his calculation of h(p”) will be h”. 3. Symmetric encryption requires the two subjects to share a common secret before communicating, which is difficult in practice. Asymmetric encryption enables the sharing of a common secret even with an eavesdropper. 4. No. Salt is stored as plaintext, and the attacker can precompute rainbow table. Upon breaking into the server, he just needs to perform calculation 𝑟 𝐗𝐎𝐑 𝑠 , which is ℎ(𝑝𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑑), then perform dictionary attack. XOR operation is very easy to perform and takes little time, so the time for the attack is not significantly extended. 5. It is a function that is easy to compute but difficult to reverse unless you have a specific piece of extra information (the "trapdoor"). In asymmetric encryption, the public key is the function, and the private key is the trapdoor. Part IV Solution: 1. Assume that the hacker uses 𝑥 seconds to test one key combination, we have: 𝑥 × 256 = 1 𝑑𝑎𝑦 To brute force all possible keys for a 112-bit key, the time will be: 𝑥 × 2112 = 𝑥 × 256 × 256 = 256 𝑑𝑎𝑦𝑠 ≈ 3.2 × 1016 𝑑𝑎𝑦𝑠
practice.02_Access_Control_Web_Security_Practice_: ISE 331: Fundamentals of Computer Security Practice Problems for Lectures 09 to 11 Directions: Below is a set of exercises and problems you should do for practice. Answering this set of questions should be just one part of your preparation for quizzes and exams. In addition to solving these problems you should: • Review the lecture notes. • Review your homework assignments. • Form a study group and test each other on the material. Note: The solution is provided on the last page. It is strongly recommended that you work on the questions first before going to the solution. Part I. Multiple Choice 1. Access control is necessary for protecting the ______ aspect(s) of a system. A. Confidentiality B. Confidentiality and Integrity C. Availability D. Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability 2. Which is a primary reason not to use Access Control Matrix in a large-scale system, like cloud data storage? A. It is inefficient due to the high percentage of empty cells. B. It is difficult to enumerate all access rights of a given user. C. It can only represent a limited number of rights. D. It does not support separating the users to different groups. 3. An administrator grants all access rights within a system which cannot be overwritten by users. This is a typical example of: A. Discretionary Access Control B. Mandatory Access Control C. Role-based Access Control D. Rule-based Access Control 4. Which is NOT a goal of browser sandboxing? A. Protect the computer system and the user from web attackers. B. Isolate websites of different origins from each other. C. Achieve platform independence so browsers can run on different computers. D. Separate the rest of the computer system from the browser. 5. A website bank.com includes a JavaScript script from advertisement.com. What is the origin when the script executes? A. The origin is bank.com. B. The origin is advertisement.com. C. The origin is neither bank.com nor advertisement.com. D. The script will not be executed because of the Same Origin Policy (SOP). 6. Which choice correctly describes what can a website do according to the Same Origin Policy (SOP)? A. A website can only send and read information to/from other websites of the same origin. B. A website can send information to all websites, but can only read responses from the same origin . C. A website can read responses from all websites, but can only send information to same origin websites. D. A website can only read information from other websites of the same origin, but cannot send information. 7. You received a cookie from http://login.safetravel.com when you log in. Which choice is correct regarding this cookie? A. The cookie can be used to authenticate you the next time you visit this website. B. Your browser will send this cookie when you visit www.airtravel.com. C. If the cookie is lost or stolen, you will not be able to login to this website again. D. The cookie was encrypted by the server before it was sent to you, 8. Which option made CSRF attack possible? A. The attacker can steal your login information if you use http instead of https. B. The server will ignore cookie verification as long as the request is correct. C. The server cannot distinguish between same-site and cross-site requests. D. Your browser will send the same cookie to different websites. 9. An attacker uploaded a modified image as his avatar on a social media website. The modified image contains malicious code, and other users who load this image in their browser will add the attacker as a friend. This is: A. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) B. Stored Cross-Site Scripting (Stored XSS) C. Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (Reflected XSS) D. SQL Injection 10. Which choice is NOT correct regarding SQL Injection? A. It affects the server instead of the users’ browsers. B. Properly sanitizing user inputs can help reduce the likelihood of a SQL injection. C. The attacker only needs to know one user’s username to start the attack. D. It can be done without knowing the structure of http requests sent to the server. 11. What is the defining characteristic of a third-party cookie compared to a first-party cookie? A. It is only used for session management and authentication. B. It belongs to the domain of embedded content, such as an iframe or image. C. It is stored permanently on the hard drive, while first-party cookies are temporary. D. It can only be read by the server and not the browser. Part II. True or False 1. The “no write up, no read down” rule is more suitable for a system where the integrity of the information is valued more. 2. The Access Control List model is more suitable for distributed systems, like door locks for hotel rooms. 3. Capabilities are unforgeable tokens of authority that are bind to the object being accessed. 4. https://www.safe.com/home/ and https://login.safe.com/home/ have the same origin according to the Same Origin Policy (SOP). 5. A website games.cherry.com can set cookie for all websites with a domain suffix of cherry.com. 6. Cookies are used to provide an additional authentication method when users login to a website a second time. 7. If you accidentally opened an attacker’s website, you will be safe as long as you don’t click any links on this website. 8. Reflected XSS can be stopped if the server stops echoing user input. 9. Replacing user input with escape characters (like using /” instead of ”) can help prevent SQL injection. 10. For Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) to be successful, the attacker needs to know the user’s cookie. 11. A third-party tracker can only track you if you visit their website directly at least once. 12. Browser fingerprinting can identify a user even if they have disabled all cookies. Part III. Short Answer 1. The Bell-LaPadula model and the Biba model aim to protect different aspects of information in a system. Provide an example of an action that is acceptable in one system but unacceptable in the other, with proper explanation. 2. A user logged into his bank website, and accidentally opened an attacker’s website at the same time. Explain what could happen without the Same Origin Policy (SOP). 3. Assume that your cookie for a website was probably stolen a few seconds ago. Your classmate Samy recommended you to immediately sign out from the website. Will that help or not? Explain. 4. List one similarity and one difference between Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and SQL Injection. 5. After logging in to a social media website, Bob accidentally clicked the link to an attacker’s website. While it seems that nothing happened on the attacker's website, he noticed that he has added a number of friends on the social media website. What type of attack has Bob most likely experienced? Come up with one approach to stop this type of attack that can be done on the browser end. 6. Alice and Samy both have accounts on Elgg.com. Elgg.com is a social media website that allows users to make posts. Those posts are stored on Elgg.com servers. 1) Samy makes an Elgg.com post with the contents (.js files contain JavaScript code): <script src="http://Elggmail.com/something.js"></script> Assume Elgg.com does not check user inputs. If Alice opens Samy’s post, what would be its origin? 2) Which of the following statements is true about Alice opening Samy’s post? Explain. a) Alice’s browser is able to make a request to Elggmail.com/something.js without being blocked b) If Elgg.com sanitized all HTML input, Alice’s browser would not run something.js. 3) Elgg.com has a reset password functionality that can be triggered by accessing http://Elgg.com/resetPassword. It makes a request that sets the currently logged-in user’s password to the "password" query parameter input. Assume Elgg.com does not check user inputs. What attack can Samy launch using this setup? Describe what they need to post to achieve this. Part IV. Calculation 1. A cloud data storage company has eight million users, and hosts a total of one billion files. Assume storing the access rights of one user on one file needs two bytes. Answer the following questions with the approximation 103 = 210 : 1) How much storage space is necessary for this company to store all access rights using access control matrix? 2) Assume that on average, one file is shared with 40 users. How much storage space is necessary to store all access rights using access control list? Part I Solution: 1-5 DABCA 6-10 BACBC 11 B Part II Solution: 1-5 TFFFT 6-10 FFTTF 11-12 FT Part III Solution: 1. In the Bell-LaPadula model, someone with a lower security level can “write up”, creating information with a higher security level. However, in the Biba model, there is the rule of “no write up”, prohibiting someone with a lower security level to create information with a higher security level. 2. Without the Same Origin Policy, there will be no constraints for a website to read responses and information from a different website. In that case, the attacker website can read the information on the user ’s bank website, and also read responses sent from the bank website to the user, obtaining personal information. 3. Signing off immediately will help prevent any further damage, since signing off terminates the current session and tells the server to stop using the current cookie. If an attacker is currently sending request to the server with the cookie, his request will no longer be accepted. 4. Similarity: 1. Both are caused by failure to separate data from code. 2. Both are caused by unsanitized user input. Differences: 1. XSS happens on the user’s browser (client-side, or frontend), while SQL injection happens on the database server (server-side, or backend). 2. XSS scripts are written with browser -executable languages, like JavaScript, while SQL injection scripts are written with SQL, as the name suggests. 5. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is the most likely. To stop this type of attack from the browser end, the browser can always attach the originating site when sending a request to the server. Also, the browser can assist the server by implementing the SameSite Attribute, which prevents the browser from sending cookies with cross -site requests when it is set to Strict. 6. 1) Elgg.com. 2) a) True, same-origin policy doesn’t stop sending requests to other websites. b) True, Samy’s post would no longer be interpreted as HTML, just plain text. 3) CSRF attack. Luring Alice to visit his website that contains a modified link, Samy can trick Alice into making a request and attaching cookies to cause an unintended password reset. Part IV Solution: 1. 1) 8 × 106 × 109 × 2 = 1.6 × 1016 𝑏𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠 = 16000 𝑇𝐵 (𝑜𝑟 16 𝑃𝐵) 2) 109 × 40 × 2 = 8 × 1010 𝑏𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠 = 80𝐺𝐵
practice.03_Network_Security_Practice_Questions_S: ISE 331: Fundamentals of Computer Security Practice Problems for Lectures 13 to 17 (Network Security) Directions: Below is a set of exercises and problems you should do for practice. Answering this set of questions should be just one part of your preparation for quizzes and exams. In addition to solving these problems you should: • Review the lecture notes. • Review your homework assignments. • Form a study group and test each other on the material. Note: The solution is provided on the last page. It is strongly recommended that you work on the questions first before going to the solution. Part I. Multiple Choice 1. For standard DNS, which attack is the most difficult to perform? A. Fake DNS responses on local network B. Use malware to add entries in /etc/hosts C. Poison cache for NS record in local DNS server D. Take over generic top-level domain DNS server 2. Which is incorrect regarding Query ID in a DNS packet? A. It was originally a functionality mechanism, later became an implicit security mechanism B. A DNS response that contains a non-matching Query ID will be dropped C. An attacker cannot forge a valid DNS response if he does not know the original Query ID D. It is a 16-bit number located at the beginning of a DNS packet 3. An on-path attacker wants to fake DNS response from the local DNS server to the client. Which might be an obstacle? A. The attacker cannot observe the traffic between the local DNS server and the Root Nameservers B. The attacker cannot guess the correct Query ID in the request sent by the client C. The attacker cannot match the destination and source port numbers D. The attacker cannot make the fake response arrive at the client soon enough 4. You queried local DNS server for the A record of www.example.com. Assume the relevant information is already in cache, which is correct? A. The local DNS server will still communicate with the nameserver of example.com for confirmation B. The local DNS server will send you a response containing the IPv4 address of www.example.com C. An attacker within local network cannot fake the response from the local DNS server to you D. An attacker can poison the cache of the local DNS server if his response arrives before your query 5. Which description best fits an Autonomous System (AS) in the context of Internet routing and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)? A. A type of server that handles BGP requests on the Internet. B. A single router that handles all Internet traffic for a specific country or region. C. An administrative entity that manages a collection of IP prefixes on the Internet. D. A security protocol used for data encryption and authentication on the Internet. 6. In standard BGP, an attacker announces a fake route to attract Internet traffic. Which of the following is incorrect? A. The attacker can drop all traffic and cause blackholing. B. The attacker can eavesdrop on traffic passing through the fake route. C. The attacker can modify passing certificates without being detected. D. The attacker can drop packets selectively and make the connection instable. 7. To prevent or stop Denial of Service (DoS) attack as the victim, ____ is not a valid option. A. Perform ingress filtering near the victim B. Stop responding to requests sent by all users C. Use anti-DoS protection provided by companies like Cloudflare D. Acquire more resources to deal with the attacks 8. To delay the calculus exam, the attacker used his botnet of 600,000 IP cameras all over the world to send requests to the university’s website at the same time. This is a(n) ____. A. Amplified Denial of Service Attack B. Application-layer Denial of Service Attack C. Distributed Denial of Service Attack D. Reflected Denial of Service Attack 9. Which is NOT a feature of worms in computer security? A. Self-evolution B. Self-propagation C. Self-replication D. Can carry payload 10. In a network where most internal hosts are behind a firewall that blocks incoming traffic, which targeting strategy would likely be the best for a worm trying to spread internally? A. Local subnet scanning B. Hit-list scanning C. Pseudorandom scanning D. Random scanning 11. A Network-based IDS (NIDS) performs TCP stream reassembly before applying signature -based detection. Why is this step necessary? A. It can reduce data size by deleting encapsulation headers. B. It can decrypt the message and prepare plaintext for signature matching. C. It can remove separators to combine segmented messages. D. It can convert other protocols’ traffic to TCP for content analysis. 12. An organization deploys an anomaly -based IDS in a n environment where user behavior changes frequently . What is the most likely operational challenge? A. The IDS has difficulty detecting a long list of attack signatures. B. The IDS suffers from a high rate of false positives. C. The IDS needs a great amount of computing power to analyze anomalies. D. The IDS cannot predict frequently changing user behaviors. 13. Which firewall policy matches the Least Privilege Principle? A. Default-allow: Drop only known malicious ports and protocols. B. Default-deny: Drop all traffic except for specifically accepted ones. C. Dynamic-allow: Open ports automatically when a host requests them. D. Egress-only: Only allow traffic leaving the network. 14. What is the primary advantage of a stateful firewall over a stateless firewall? A. It can combine segmented messages for better situational awareness. B. It takes significantly less computing power to achieve similar results. C. It can track the state of a connection to allow for more detailed policies. D. It does not need to track a connection on different ports. 15. ( D ) Alice wants to send an encrypted message to Bob with asymmetric encryption. She needs to: (2 pts) A. Encrypt the message with her secret key B. Encrypt the message with her public key C. Encrypt the message with Bob’s secret key D. Encrypt the message with Bob’s public key 3. ( A ) Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is necessary for secure asymmetric encryption because: (2 pts) A. There’s no way to authenticate a public key without PKI B. There’s no way to exchange a secret key without PKI C. PKI is necessary for public and secret key pair generation D. PKI is necessary for switching to asymmetric encryption from symmetric encryption 4. (Short Answer, 4 pts) Alice and Bob are your classmates. One day Bob told you that he is trying to express his love to Alice, but he is too afraid to speak out openly and will only send the hash of his message to Alice, with a well-known publicly available hash algorithm. You doubted because you know hashing is one-way. However, a few days later Bob showed up with Alice, and said that Alice had learnt the message, they are now lovers. Can you explain what probably happened with your knowledge of cryptography and passwords? Solution: The most probable explanation is that Alice is attempting something similar to a dictionary attack. She guessed a few possible short messages like “iloveyou” “I love you”, calculated their hash, compared them against the hash send by Bob and found a match. Not necessary in your answer: Of course, this only works if Alice knows Bob’s intention.

(Short Answer/Calculation, 4 pts) Your classmate posted the hash of: (his credit card number (16 digits) ⊕ PIN number (4 digits) ) on TikTok/Douyin and said “This is the SHA-256 hash of my credit card number and PIN number combination. You cannot know the number because hash is one-way.” Is this true for the following two conditions? Assume calculating SHA-256 hash of a 20-digit number on an average PC takes 1 microsecond (10−6s), and numbers 0-9 for every digit are equally likely. 1) The attacker doesn’t know anything about his credit card. 2) The attacker knows his credit card number. Note: The ⊕ symbol means concatenation, 12345678 ⊕ 910 = 12345678910 Solution: For both conditions, the attacker can try something like a dictionary attack, calculating the hash of all possible digit combinations until he sees a match. 1) 1020 total combinations for the 20-digit number, brute forcing all the possible combinations takes 1014 seconds. You should know that 105 seconds are roughly a day, so it takes 109 days or at least a few million years to try all combinations, so the classmate is technically true. 2) In this case, all 16 digits in front are known, and the attacker just need to try 104 combinations. Brute forcing takes only 10-2 seconds or 0.01s. The classmate is definitely wrong.

(2 pts) A. https://games.site.com/game1/ and http://games.site.com/game1/ B. http://login.site.com/ and http://www.site.com/ C. http://www.eshop.com/item=1245 and http://www.eshop.com/cart/add?id=1245 D. https://www.bing.cn/ and https://www.bing.com/ 3. ( C ) Which attack involves an attacker tricking a user’s browser into sending information to a site where the user is authenticated, often without the user’s knowledge? (2 pts) A. SQL Injection B. Reflective Cross‑Site Scripting (Reflective XSS) C. Cross‑Site Request Forgery (CSRF) D. Stored Cross‑Site Scripting (Stored XSS) 4. (Short Answer, 4 pts) Bob experienced CSRF attack and lost some money. He understands the other parts of the attack, but still doesn’t understand why the bank cannot notice something went wrong. In his mind, the bank should know that he clicked the link on the attacker’s website, instead of on the bank’s website. Explain this part to Bob. Solution: The bank cannot tell the difference because both a click on the bank website and a click from an attacker’s website result in the same message sent from the browser to the bank, consisting of the request itself and the cookie. The bank only receives the request and the cookie, and cannot tell the origin of the click.

(Short Answer, 4 pts) Samy always signs off immediately after he finishes what he needs to do on a website. Will this reduce the possibility of a successful CSRF attack? Explain. Solution: Yes. The sign-off terminates the current session, rendering the cookie useless. CSRF can only be successful if the victim has a valid cookie. By signing off immediately, even if he later visits a malicious website and sends a forged request, it will not be authenticated.
